Kostka and Payne: Tonal Harmony

Modulation examples from chapters 18 and 19, with Roman numerals under the notes

Fifteen modulation examples from chapters 18 and 19 of Kostka, Payne and Almén’s Tonal Harmony, from Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky, with the Roman-numeral analysis under the notes (When in Rome). Play each one.

Fifteen examples from Stefan Kostka, Dorothy Payne and Byron Almén’s Tonal Harmony: chapter 18, “Modulations Using Diatonic Common Chords”, and chapter 19, “Some Other Modulatory Techniques”. Most are from real pieces (Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Dvořák, Tchaikovsky); 18-2, 18-3a and 18-3b are short progressions.

How to read the labels and use the scores: Analysed Scores. For modulation itself, see Chapter 22.

Chapter 18

18-2. B♭ major to C minor

18-3a. G major to F major

18-3b. G major to F major

18-4. Mozart, Viennese Sonatina no.6, II

18-6. Tchaikovsky, Mazurka, op. 39, no. 10

18-7. Dvořák, String Quartet, op. 51, IV

Chapter 19

19-1. Beethoven, Piano Sonata, op. 14, no.2

19-2. Schubert, Five Piano Pieces, D. 459, no. 3

19-3. Beethoven, Piano Sonata, op. 53

19-4. Schubert, Piano Sonata, D. 850, III

19-5. Mozart, Fantasia, K. 475

19-6. Beethoven, Symphony no. 4, op. 60

19-10. Bach, Partita no. 2 for Solo Violin, “Gigue”

19-11. Bach, Für Freuden, lasst uns springen

19-12. Mozart, Fantasia, K. 475, mm 6-16 (simplified)

NoteFor teachers
  • Source: the notes and analyses are the DDMAL Key Modulation Dataset’s encodings of the book’s examples (Néstor Nápoles López and others), translated automatically to RomanText and copied into When in Rome. scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs reads the MusicXML (src/kostka), and every note was checked against music21’s reading of the same files.
  • Copyright: the book is in copyright. The pieces are public domain; 18-2, 18-3a and 18-3b are progressions as encoded in the dataset, and 19-12 is the book’s simplification of bars 6–16 of Mozart’s Fantasia, K. 475.
  • Not shown: grace notes (19-1, 19-3) are left out of the scores.
  • Not edited: the analyses are an automated translation and are shown as they are.

For students

Gotham, Mark, et al. When in Rome: A Meta-Corpus of Functional Harmony. GitHub. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome. The analyses on this page (RomanText files), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Hutchinson, Robert. “Modulation.” Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom, ch. 22, U of Puget Sound. musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html. Tonicization against modulation, closely related keys, diatonic and chromatic pivot chords, and direct, common-tone and sequential modulation.

Kostka, Stefan, Dorothy Payne, and Byron Almén. Tonal Harmony. 8th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2018. Table of contents. highered.mheducation.com/sites/0078025141/information_center_view0/table_of_contents.html. Chapters 18 (Modulations Using Diatonic Common Chords) and 19 (Some Other Modulatory Techniques), the source of the examples on the Kostka and Payne page.

For teachers

Nápoles López, Néstor, et al. Key Modulation Dataset. GitHub (DDMAL). github.com/DDMAL/key_modulation_dataset. The encodings and analyses of the textbook examples, translated to RomanText by Nápoles López and copied into When in Rome.
